name: Karl Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two five-axis CNC machines at Ardent Precision, a machine shop that makes small metal parts for aircraft seats and hospital beds. A CNC is a cutting machine that follows a program, so my day is loading blanks, setting tools, checking the first part with gauges and keeping both machines cutting. I'm the senior on days, so the two apprentices come to me. The best bit is a tricky titanium part coming off perfect first time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned programs. How much of your day is screen work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Maybe a fifth of it. I tweak the programs at the machine, and I've started pasting bits of the code into an AI chatbot to check for mistakes before I run them. It's caught two crashes this year that would've cost thousands. The rest is hands-on: swarf, coolant, gauges and a lot of standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that would be a bit disappointing for me, to be honest. I've been having fun with the AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the hype was overblown but the tools are still handy, because they are. With friends I'd say the real fight was always about wages and hours, not AI. Online I'd keep posting about the four-day week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The chatbot would still catch my code mistakes, and the machines still need someone like me. It'd just mean I'd been a bit too excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools every day and keep teaching the apprentices. I'd finish the robot programming certificate I'm doing online anyway, because the shop has a robot arm loading one machine already. And I'd keep putting £250 a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a big match that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the robot arm doing in your shop now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It loads blanks into the newest machine overnight, so we get eight hours of cutting with nobody there. I set it up with the rep last spring. The robot arm in our shop didn't cost anyone a job, it just means we take more orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. Amira, my girlfriend, and I pay £1,100 a month for a flat that's too small. But that's life everywhere, it's not about AI.

say: I'd say the hype was **overblown** but the tools are still **handy**.
I'd keep posting that the real fight is **wages and hours**.
think: The chatbot still catches **code mistakes**, and the shop still needs me.
I'd only have been **too excited**, nothing worse.
do: Keep using **AI code checks** every day.
feel: **Calm**, a bit flat, like a match ending **nil-nil**.
S0.quote: The robot arm in our shop didn't cost anyone a job, it just means we take more orders.
fieldNote: He is already an **everyday AI user** and sees it as a safety tool.
His only pressure here is **high rent**, which he treats as normal.
He set up the shop's **robot arm** himself, which shapes his confidence.

steps.text: Keep checking CNC programs with the AI chatbot before running
Finish the online robot programming certificate this winter
Save £250 a month towards a bigger flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I actually expect, I think. Thinking work first, robots slower. Machine shops will feel it in the office before the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should get ahead of it, not fight it. To friends I'd say the gains have to be shared. A robot should mean a shorter week, not a smaller team. I'd post that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well out of this. The quoting and the programming will be done by software, but someone has to make sure the robot cells and the machines actually work together. That's the job I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ardent to make me the cell lead for the robot loading, with a pay rise to match. I'd do a proper course in industrial robot integration at the technical college, which is about £1,400. And I'd push for the shop's first union recognition vote, because nobody else there will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. Slightly guilty about being excited, because I know not everyone's going to land on their feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of, when you say not everyone lands on their feet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray in quoting. He's 58 and does all our prices by hand from drawings. Software will do that in seconds. He's taught me loads, and I don't know what he does next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want a union vote. How do you think the owners would react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd hate it at first. But they need me for the robot cell, so I've got some weight to throw around. Better to use it for everyone than just for my own pay rise.

say: I'd say we should **get ahead** of the change, not fight it.
I'd push for robots to bring a **shorter week**, not a smaller team.
think: Software takes quoting and programming, but someone must make **cells work** together.
That **integration job** is the one I want.
do: Ask to become **robot cell lead** with a pay rise.
Pay **£1,400** for a college course in robot integration.
Start the shop's first **union recognition** vote.
feel: **Excited**, and slightly **guilty** that others won't land well.
S1.quote: A robot should mean a shorter week, not a smaller team.
fieldNote: He expects to **gain** from this scenario and admits it openly.
He wants to use his new **bargaining power** for others, not just himself.
His worry is for older colleagues like **Ray in quoting**.

steps.text: Ask Ardent for the robot cell lead role and a raise
Pay £1,400 for the robot integration course at college
Organise the shop's first union recognition vote

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's different. If the AI can do any thinking work by 2028, then it can do my robot integration plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when governments have to share the gains directly, like a payment to everyone from a tax on the big AI firms. I'd say it at work and I'd be posting it every day. Retraining won't cut it on its own if there's two years' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the part of my job I'm proudest of, the programming and setup, goes first. By 2028 an AI writes better CNC code than me. I'd still have the hands-on bit until robots arrive around 2031, but that's the boring part. And Amira's an architect, so her job's thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every AI tool going and become the person who supervises them at Ardent, because that's still a job for a couple of years. I'd save hard, £500 a month instead of £250. And I'd join a campaign for a basic income funded by an AI tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit dizzy. I've always been the one who's ahead, and in AGI by 2028 there's nowhere to be ahead of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Amira talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we stay in the city. If both our jobs are shaky by 2031, the £1,100 rent makes no sense. Her parents have a house with a spare room an hour away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn every AI tool. Does that really protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For two or three years, maybe. After that, probably not. It buys time and money, and I'd use the money to give us a cushion while we work out what's next.

say: I'd call for a **payment to everyone** funded by an AI tax.
I'd say **retraining alone** won't work with two years' notice.
think: My **programming and setup** skills go first, by 2028.
My partner Amira's **architecture job** is thinking work too, so both incomes are at risk.
do: Become Ardent's **AI supervisor** to stay useful for a few years.
Join a campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: **Anxious and dizzy**, with **nowhere** to be ahead of.
S2.quote: I've always been the one who's ahead, and in AGI by 2028 there's nowhere to be ahead of.
fieldNote: Fast AGI removes his usual **advantage** of being early.
He notices the **thinking parts** of his job go before the hands-on parts.
His partner's exposure makes this a **household** worry, not just his.

steps.text: Become the shop's go-to person for AI-run machine programming
Join a campaign for a basic income from an AI tax
Talk with Amira about moving to her parents' spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI, and then robots in 2034. That's long enough to do something with, if you move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: tax the AI firms and share it out. But with five years I'd also say workers should be buying in, like co-ops that own the robots. I'd talk about that at the pub and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think five years is enough for me to build something. If I can run a small robot shop with a couple of mates, we're owners, not employees. That's the progressive bit and the selfish bit at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot integration course in the first year, then save towards a small machine shop with Dev and Tom from Ardent, as a co-op. I'd want £15,000 between us to start, plus a loan. And I'd keep pushing the union at Ardent in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. It's a gamble, and I like gambles more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op actually make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short runs for local firms, the jobs the big shops won't touch. Brackets, repair parts, prototypes. With good robots, three of us could do what fifteen did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the co-op when robots match people around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we own the robots, which is the whole point. If the work's done by machines, I'd rather be the one who owns a few of them than the one who got replaced.

say: I'd say workers should **own the robots** through co-ops.
I'd keep calling for an **AI tax** shared with everyone.
think: Five years is enough to **build something** as an owner.
Owning a robot shop is both **progressive and selfish**.
do: Take the **robot integration** course in the first year.
Save **£15,000** with two colleagues for a co-op shop.
Keep pushing for a **union** at Ardent meanwhile.
feel: **Uneasy but excited** about a gamble he likes.
S3.quote: If the work's done by machines, I'd rather be the one who owns a few of them than the one who got replaced.
fieldNote: He turns the five-year window into a **business plan**.
He blends progressive ideals with **self-interest** and says so.
He enjoys **risk** more than most people his age.

steps.text: Take the robot integration course at college in year one
Save £15,000 with Dev and Tom for a co-op machine shop
Fit the co-op shop with robot loaders on every machine
Keep organising for a union at Ardent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. I'd be nearly forty by then. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually get the politics right, so let's use it. Four-day week, shared ownership, proper retraining. I'd say that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relaxed. Ten years is two careers' worth for me. I'd ride the wave rather than worry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ardent for a few years, become the robot cell lead and learn everything. Around 2030 I'd open the co-op shop with Dev and Tom. Amira and I would buy a small house in the meantime, because by then we'd have the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would shake that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big firms bought up everything before small shops got a look in. That's my one fear. That's why I'd want the government to stop monopolies early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a house. What changes for Amira's job in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have time to move into something like planning approvals or site work, which is more people-facing. We talked about it once over dinner, and she's less worried than me, funnily enough.

say: I'd say this decade lets us **get the politics** right.
I'd push for a **four-day week** and shared ownership.
think: Ten years is **two careers'** worth for me at my age.
I'd **ride the wave** rather than worry about where it lands.
Privately, I would feel **relaxed** about this picture.
do: Become **robot cell lead** at Ardent first.
S4.quote: Ten years is two careers' worth for me. I'd ride the wave rather than worry about it.
fieldNote: A decade makes him **confident**, almost relaxed, about his own prospects.
His remaining fear is **monopoly**, not technology.
His partner is **less worried** than he is, he says.

steps.text: Take the robot cell lead role at Ardent
Open the co-op machine shop with Dev and Tom around 2030
Buy a small house with Amira using the saved deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Everything I'm good at, being early, being handy with the tools, stops counting. What would help is a share of the gains for everyone, paid from a tax on AI firms, so nobody's left with nothing while it settles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the machines. Every answer comes back to that. Robots aren't the enemy; an owner who keeps every penny they save is.

headlineQuote: Robots aren't the enemy; an owner who keeps every penny they save is.
portrait: Karl is a 27-year-old **CNC setter** at a precision machine shop making aircraft and hospital parts.
He uses **AI daily** to check his code and set up the shop's first robot loader.
He is calm in slower scenarios and plans a worker-owned **co-op shop**.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious**, because his early-mover advantage disappears and his partner's job is exposed.
He frames everything around **who owns** the machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being early and skilled with AI stops counting.
whatWouldHelp: A **share of AI gains** for everyone, paid from a tax on AI firms.
